title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why start from decision points rather than from systems?
options: Because decision points are easier to enumerate
Because a system inventory built from a software inventory inherits its blind spots — including sourcing and selection for reduction
Because regulators define obligations by decision type
Because systems change more often than decisions do
questions.explanation: The question "what AI do we use" gets answered with what somebody bought. Sourcing (who sees the posting at all) shapes the applicant pool before anyone applies, and is skipped constantly.

questions.prompt: Why is a manager's weekend scoring spreadsheet an automated employment decision tool?
options: Because spreadsheets contain formulas, which are algorithms
Because it ranks people against criteria and determines outcomes — and it will be produced in discovery, despite having no vendor, contract or procurement record
Because most regulations define AEDTs to include any software
It isn't — the definition requires machine learning
questions.explanation: No procurement record is exactly why it needs to be on your inventory. It is also, in a reduction, likely to be the highest-stakes scoring instrument in the organization.

options: Systems purchased by departments outside HR
Unapproved tools employees use without permission
AI capability delivered inside products bought before the capability existed — no procurement event, no owner who thinks of it as AI, no documentation, and frequently on by default
Vendors' subprocessors and downstream model providers
questions.explanation: Which means the deployment decision may have been made by a vendor's product team rather than by anyone in your organization.

questions.prompt: Why do the five discovery questions avoid the word "AI"?
options: Because the term is legally ambiguous
Because asking "do you use AI" gets a no from people configuring a tool — the questions route around the word by asking about scores, sorts, release notes and defaults
Because vendors dispute whether their products qualify
Because it avoids alarming stakeholders
questions.explanation: "Is there a default sort, and is it chronological?" gets an answer. "Do you use AI in screening?" gets a denial from someone who genuinely believes it.

questions.prompt: A recruiter reviews 400 applications in 90 minutes against a ranked list, without seeing the ranking rationale. Which of the four questions does this fail?
options: Authority and incentive
Information and time — they cannot see why the system ranked as it did, and fourteen seconds per item is enough to confirm an ordering, not challenge one
Time only
None — the review is genuine as long as they can override
questions.explanation: And note that the time question is arithmetic rather than opinion, which is why it most often produces an uncomfortable silence in the room.

questions.prompt: Why does the incentive question matter?
options: Because reviewers should be compensated for review work

Because reviewers who follow the system and get a bad outcome are fine, while reviewers who override it and get a bad outcome are answerable — so the structure punishes the behaviour you're claiming as your safeguard
Because incentives determine how much time reviewers allocate
Because performance metrics are themselves an AEDT
questions.explanation: Along with authority, it's the usual failing pair. Most of these failures are fixable: time can be budgeted, authority granted, rationale surfaced. What can't be fixed is a review layer nobody ever examined.

questions.prompt: What does Connecticut's framework do beyond removing the tool as a defence `[V]`?
options: It requires annual third-party audits of all AEDTs
It creates a private right of action for algorithmic discrimination
It makes evidence of anti-bias testing a mitigating factor, and identifies what gets weighed — quality, efficacy, recency, scope, results, and the employer's response to them
It prohibits AEDTs in hiring decisions entirely
questions.explanation: Which is close to a specification rather than general encouragement. Statutory framework effective 1 October 2026; principal compliance obligations from 1 October 2027.

questions.prompt: Under that framework, why is testing that found a disparity and produced no action worse than not testing?
options: Because it wastes resources that could fund remediation
Because the employer's response to results is among the factors weighed — so you have documented knowledge and inaction in the same file
Because untested systems are presumed compliant
Because testing without remediation violates the notice requirements
questions.explanation: It is the factor an organization can most easily fail, and it is why Module 3 asks you to decide what you'll do with a bad result *before* you have one.
